howto.h2: Tuning with your microphone, step by step
items: Allow microphone access in your browser. Nothing to install, and nothing leaves your device: the analysis runs locally.
Pick the mode matching your instrument. The mode narrows detection to a tight range around the expected strings, which rules out mains hum and high-frequency noise.
Play an open string and let it ring: a sustained note measures far better than a sharply plucked one.
Bring the needle to zero. The scale is graduated in cents, from −50 to +50.
Work from the lowest string to the highest, then go round again: changing one string changes the tension on the neck, so the others drift slightly.
howto.octave: One detail that prevents a lot of mistakes: in instrument mode, a frequency detected an octave away is folded back onto the right string. You cannot tune a string a full octave too high without noticing — the classic trap of chromatic tuners.

frequencies.intro: These values are not copied from a table: they are computed from the 440 Hz reference A using equal temperament. They are exactly the targets the tuner aims for.
frequencies.caption: Standard tunings offered, from the lowest string to the highest
frequencies.note: The guitar offers three alternative tunings alongside standard: drop D, half a step down, and open G. The other instruments use standard tuning; for anything else, chromatic mode still works.

chromatic.body: Chromatic mode listens from 40 to 1,500 Hz and shows the nearest note, without assuming a target string. It comes in handy whenever the instrument is not on the list: voice, harmonica, brass, strings deliberately tuned off standard, or simply to check a pitch.

cents.body: A semitone is 100 cents, so the scale covers one semitone either side of the target note. Beyond fifty cents the tuner switches to the neighbouring note: if the note shown is not the one you expect, you are more than a semitone off.
cents.tip: A piece of luthier advice that holds for every string instrument: arrive at the note from below. A string loosened and then brought up holds its tuning far better than one overtightened and released.

faq.q1: Why does the microphone miss my low string?
faq.a1: A bass low E sounds at 41.20 Hz, below the useful range of many phone and laptop microphones. Play closer to the microphone, or tune that string on its twelfth-fret harmonic, one octave higher.
faq.q2: Is the ukulele G really higher than the C?
faq.a2: Yes, and the table above shows it: the G sounds at 392 Hz, the C at 261.63 Hz. That is re-entrant tuning, specific to the ukulele — the strings do not run low to high. It is not a tuning mistake.
faq.q3: Should I prefer a clip-on tuner?
faq.a3: In rehearsal or on stage, yes: a clip reads the vibration of the wood and ignores ambient noise. Here the microphone listens, which assumes a reasonably quiet room. At home the difference is negligible.

links.chordDetect: Identify a chord played into the microphone

library.intro: The library gathers {total} hand-written diagrams across six instruments. Each instrument covers the same harmonic families on all twelve roots, so that no common chord is missing.
library.caption: Diagrams available per instrument
library.families: Families covered: major, minor, 7, maj7, min7, diminished, augmented, sus2 and sus4. Piano adds sus and add9 chords. Bass shows the root only: on four low strings a full chord sounds muddy, and bass players work the foundation note.
library.note: These positions are deliberately limited to the main fingerings, not every possible variation. A chord missing, or a mistake? Write to us and we will fix it.

extended.body: Beyond the catalogue, {formulas} extended chord formulas are computed on the fly across the twelve roots: ninths, elevenths, thirteenths, m7b5, dim7, mMaj7 and altered chords. That is why a chord absent from the diagrams still appears when it turns up in a chart.
extended.body2: The number of positions actually produced varies by instrument: some combinations have no playable fingering on four strings while they do on six. The table above gives the exact count, instrument by instrument.

reading.strings: On a string instrument the diagram shows the neck head-on: strings as columns, frets as rows. Dots mark where the fingers go. A cross above a string means it must not ring, a circle means it is played open. When the chord does not start at the nut, the starting fret is shown at the side.
reading.piano: On piano the diagram shows a fragment of keyboard with the keys to press. Notes run from lowest to highest, in the most natural position for the right hand.

notation.body: Two systems name the same notes. The American system uses letters, inherited from Anglo-Saxon notation; the Latin system uses the syllables of Guido of Arezzo, in use across France, Italy and Spain. They refer to exactly the same pitches.
notation.caption: Correspondence between the two notations
notation.body2: Alviena accepts both when you type: enter “Lam” or “Am” and you get the same chord. Display follows the preference set in your profile and switches everywhere at once. Charts, however, are always stored in American notation — which is what lets you change the display without ever losing anything.
notation.minor: For minor chords, French adds “m” just as American does: A minor is written “Lam” or “Am”.

enharmony.body: C sharp and D flat name the same pitch and use the same fingering. This is called enharmonic equivalence. The choice between the two spellings still matters: it depends on the key of the piece, and a well-written score stays consistent.
enharmony.body2: When you transpose a chart, Alviena applies a simple rule: the keys of F, B flat, E flat, A flat, D flat and G flat are written with flats; the others with sharps. A chord originally written with a flat keeps that spelling. This is what stops you reading “A sharp” where every musician expects “B flat”.

slash.body: A chord written G/B reads “G over B”: the G chord, played with a B in the bass. This notation writes a bass line that walks down or up underneath chords that do not themselves move — common in songwriting and pop alike.
slash.body2: Transposition handles both halves of the chord. A G/B moved up a tone becomes A/C#, not A/B. Many transposition tools miss this detail, and the bass line breaks when they do.

find.h2: Finding a chord whose name you do not know
find.body: There are two routes. You can select the notes you hear, or see under your fingers, and let the library suggest matching chords. Or play the chord into your microphone and let recognition do the work.

custom.body: If a position is missing you can draw it yourself while editing a chart: place your fingers on the neck, name the chord, and it will be saved with the chart and shown in its place wherever it appears.

links.detect: Identify a chord with your microphone
links.tuner: Tune your instrument before you play

byInstrument.h2: One page per chord, instrument by instrument
byInstrument.body: Every chord in the library has its own page: the diagram, the notes it is built from, the shape string by string, neighbouring chords, and the charts on the site that use it. Banjo and bass are not covered yet.

items: The microphone feeds a spectral analysis, folded into a chromagram: twelve pitch classes, one per note, regardless of the octave played.
That profile is compared to chord templates, one per family and root, by similarity measurement.
A minimum score is required before a result is accepted: below it, nothing is shown rather than showing something wrong.
A majority vote over the last few analyses smooths the output — which is why the display takes a fraction of a second to settle.
The best candidates stay visible with their scores: when the tool hesitates, it says so instead of deciding for you.

recognizes.body: Twelve chord families across the twelve roots: major, minor, 7, m7, maj7, 6, m6, sus2, sus4, diminished, augmented and m7b5. Names are shown in American notation.

limits.h2: What it cannot do, and why
limits.body: A C sixth and an A minor seventh are made of exactly the same four notes. No analysis based on note content can tell them apart: only harmonic function within the piece decides, and that is not audible in an isolated chord. This is precisely why candidates are shown — you choose according to context.
limits.body2: Simple triads are slightly favoured. Without that bias a plain C major would constantly be read as a sus4 or a maj7, because the natural harmonics of the strings add notes that were never played.
limits.body3: Finally, inversions are not detected: the chromagram ignores which note sits in the bass. A C major played with an E underneath is recognised as a C major.

items: Play the chord as a block and let it ring, rather than strumming continuously.
One instrument at a time: accompaniment or drums blur the profile.
Turn off whatever is making noise around you — the analysis hears everything.
If the confidence stays low, attack the chord again rather than holding on.
A correct chord on an out-of-tune instrument will not be recognised: start by tuning.

without.h2: Identifying a chord without a microphone
without.body: In a noisy rehearsal, or simply without an instrument to hand, the library also lets you start from the notes: select the ones under your fingers and matching chords are suggested.

links.chords: See the fingering for this chord

genres.body: Public chord charts are sorted into nineteen genres. Each link below filters the catalogue.

difficulty.h2: The three difficulty levels, and how they are worked out
difficulty.body: Difficulty is not declared by the author: it is computed automatically from the chords actually present in the chart. The rule is public and fits in three lines.
items: Advanced as soon as one advanced chord appears: diminished, augmented, m7b5, mMaj, or any alteration (b5, #5, b9, #9, #11, b13), along with elevenths and thirteenths.
Intermediate from two intermediate chords — maj7, maj9, m7, m9, 7, 9 — or as soon as the chart uses ten different chords.
Easy in every other case. Sus, 7sus and add chords count as basic: they are common for beginners and pose no left-hand difficulty.
difficulty.note: A three-open-chord song is therefore always rated easy, however long it runs; a song cycling through ten different positions is rated intermediate even if each one is simple. How much there is to memorise counts as much as how hard each shape is.

filters.body: Search covers title, artist, chart author and key. Filters combine: genre, difficulty, decade. Sorting offers most recent, best rated or most viewed, plus a random pick for stumbling on something you were not looking for.

content.body: A chart reads like a simplified score: named sections — intro, verse, chorus, bridge — split into bars, each bar carrying its chords and their length in beats. Add to that the key, the tempo, a capo if any, and the diagrams for the instrument you picked.
content.body2: A single song may have several versions: a simplified chart to get started, another closer to the recording. When that happens, a dedicated page brings them together.

publish.body: Every chart you create is private by default. You can make it public — it then appears in this catalogue — or keep it unlisted: reachable by anyone with the link, invisible here. That is the right middle ground for sharing with a teacher or a band without publishing.

how.body: This directory is not maintained by hand: it is built from published charts. As soon as a chart becomes public, its artist appears here. The index is alphabetical, and an artist only shows up with at least one public chart.

page.body: Each artist page gathers every public chart for that artist, with its key, its computed difficulty and the rating given by the community. It is the natural starting point when you want to work through several songs from the same repertoire.

versions.h2: Several versions of the same song
versions.body: A well-known song often attracts several charts: one simplified, another faithful to the recording, a third transposed for a particular voice. When several versions exist, a dedicated page groups them so you pick the one that suits you rather than landing on whichever was published first.

missing.body: Nothing is pulled in automatically from an outside database: this catalogue is what musicians put into it. If an artist does not appear, nobody has published a chart yet — yours would be welcome.

importChords.h1: Import a chord chart from plain text
importChords.lead: Paste text with chords written above the lyrics and get a structured chart. Here is what the import recognises, and what it does not do.

format.body: The import accepts the format most common on tablature sites: a line of chords, the matching lyric line underneath, and sections written in brackets. You paste the text and the analysis handles the split into bars.

detect.h2: How a chord line is recognised
detect.body: A line is treated as a chord line when at least four fifths of what it contains are valid chords. That threshold matters: it lets through a line carrying a passing annotation, while ruling out a lyric line that happens to contain a word like “Am” or “Do”.

sections.body: Twelve labels are understood, in English and French alike: intro, verse, chorus, pre-chorus, bridge, outro, solo, interlude, instrumental and hook, along with the French forms couplet and refrain. Numbering is kept: “[Verse 2]” stays “Verse 2”.

durations.body: Durations are not guessed at random: they come from the alignment of the text. A single chord on its line takes the whole bar. Two to four chords are spread according to the column gaps between them in the source, which reproduces the way these files are written. Beyond four chords on one line the alignment becomes too unreliable: each chord then gets one beat and the line is split into four-beat bars.

ignored.body: Plenty of clutter sits in these files. ASCII tablature, web addresses, strumming patterns, tempo markings and difficulty or tuning headers are stripped automatically. You can paste the whole page without tidying up first.

limits.body: Two things, worth knowing before you start. Lyrics are not carried over: only the chords and the structure are. And the time signature is not inferred from the text — every imported chart arrives in four beats per bar. If your song is in three, set it afterwards in the editor.

after.body: The result is editable cell by cell: rename a section, stretch a chord over two beats, split a bar, delete one. This is the moment to put back the nuances the source text never carried.

links.photo: Transcribe a photo of a score

transpose.lead: Change the key of a song without rewriting a single bar, and understand why the result is sometimes written in sharps and sometimes in flats.

intro.body: Transposition is not a separate tool: it sits in the chart view, as a selector at the bottom of the page. Open any public chart, move up or down a semitone, and everything recalculates at once.

what.body: Transposing moves every chord by the same number of semitones. The relationships between them do not change: a progression that sounded right still does, simply higher or lower. The song stays the same, only its pitch moves.

why.body: Three reasons come up constantly. Fitting a singer’s range, so they are not straining on a song written for another voice. Avoiding barre chords by finding a key that falls on open shapes. Or accompanying a transposing instrument, whose written notes differ from the notes heard.

display.body: This is a display, not a transformation. You can transpose someone else’s chart without altering anything, and return to the written key in one click. The range runs from six semitones down to six up, which covers all twelve keys: beyond that you land back on the same chords.

spelling.body: The same sound can be written two ways, and the choice is not neutral. The rule applied is simple: the keys of F, B flat, E flat, A flat, D flat and G flat are written with flats, the others with sharps. And a chord written with a flat in the original keeps that spelling. This is what stops you reading “A sharp” where every musician expects “B flat”.

slash.body: A chord written G/B is transposed on both halves: moved up a tone it becomes A/C sharp, not A/B. The bass line therefore travels with the chords, which is the expected behaviour and one many tools miss.

capo.body: Both change the pitch, but not in the same way. A capo keeps your fingerings and raises the sound: handy for playing open shapes in a key that offers none. Transposing changes the written chords and lets you play without an accessory. On a chart the two combine: the capo is part of the song, transposition is a reading setting.

links.explore: Try it on a public chart

sheetPhoto.h1: Turn a photo of a score into a chord chart
sheetPhoto.lead: Photograph a score and get an editable chart. What the analysis reads well, what it reads badly, and what it costs.

how.body: You drop in one or more images. The analysis transcribes the score bar by bar, rebuilds its structure — sections, repeats, key, time signature — then produces a chart you can edit like any other.

formats.body: Images: JPG, PNG or WebP. Files are resized before upload, so you need not worry about the size of your photos. One thing to know: PDF is not supported. If your score is a PDF, export the pages as images first.

quality.body: Transcription quality depends directly on image quality. Lay the score flat, light it evenly, frame the whole page without cutting off staves, and avoid the shadow of your own hand. One page per image.

multipage.body: You can send several images in a single analysis: they are processed in order and produce one chart. If the analysis fails reporting a score that is too long, split it into two submissions.

quota.body: The free plan includes two analyses per month. That counter is shared between image transcription and audio analysis: two analyses in total, whichever route you take. The Pro plan makes them unlimited.

draft.h2: The result is a starting point
draft.body: This needs saying plainly: an automatic transcription is not a proofread score. Durations, extended chords and ambiguous passages are the weak spots. The chart produced is yours and can be corrected bar by bar — treat it as a first draft that spares you the typing, not as a finished result.

bands.h1: Share your repertoire with a band or a class
bands.lead: How a band works on Alviena: who sees what, how you invite people, and why one licence is enough.

create.h2: Creating a band and inviting people
create.body: You create a band by giving it a name. You then generate an invitation link, valid for seven days, and pass it on however you like: message, email, on paper. Whoever opens it joins the band, with no separate sign-up for the band itself.

roles.body: There are only two roles, deliberately. A leader manages: they change the name, description and photo, attach or remove charts, and can remove a member. A member reads the repertoire, plays, and adds charts to their own book. Whoever creates the band is a leader by default and cannot leave it — it has to be handed over or deleted first.

sharing.body: Charts attached to the band are available to every member, including ones you keep private elsewhere. That is the key point: you do not have to publish a chart to share it with your band. Setlists created in the band are shared the same way.

license.h2: One licence covers the whole band
license.body: This is the question we get most. Creating a band requires a Pro subscription, but **only the person creating it** needs one. Invited members use the shared repertoire, the setlists and stage mode on a free account. A five-piece band therefore does not pay five subscriptions.

teachers.body: The model suits teaching well. A class becomes a band: you write the chart once and every student has it in their book. Several classes become several bands, each with its own repertoire. And each student transposes on their side, for their voice or their instrument, without affecting anyone else’s version.

session.h2: Without an account or a subscription
session.body: For a one-off — a jam, a rehearsal with someone passing through — a live session avoids creating a band at all. A six-character code, valid six hours, that your guests enter without creating an account.

stageMode.h1: Stage mode: play without looking away from the chart
stageMode.lead: A full-screen setlist, synchronised across every device in the band, with accompaniment and a drum machine.

setlist.body: You set the running order in advance, then switch to stage mode: the chart fills the screen with no clutter, and you move from one song to the next with a single gesture. It is designed for a music stand or a tablet sitting on an amp.

sync.body: This is the most carefully built part. When one member starts a song, every device in the band switches to the same chart, and the playback position is computed from a shared timestamp rather than streamed continuously. Devices align their clocks with the server through a series of round trips, keeping the fastest — the same principle as computer clock synchronisation. The result: everyone sees the same bar at the same moment, even on a patchy network.

accompaniment.body: Six instruments can play at once — guitar, bass, piano, mandolin, banjo and ukulele — each in block chords or arpeggios. Tempo runs from forty to three hundred beats per minute, with a metronome you can mute without stopping playback. You can start a whole song, a section, or a single bar to work on a passage.

groove.body: Eighteen patterns across six families: rock and pop, jazz and blues, reggae and Latin, funk and soul, hip hop, country and folk. Fifteen drum voices, sampled from an eighties drum machine. Patterns are written over two bars, so the second one varies — a fill, ghost notes — instead of looping identically.

live.body: Lighter than a band: a six-character code, chosen without ambiguous letters or digits so it can be read aloud, valid for six hours. Guests join without creating an account, and any participant can push a chart to everyone else’s screen.

audioToChords.h1: Get the chords of a track from an audio file
audioToChords.lead: Submit a recording and get a first draft chart. Read this first: what the analysis actually returns.

expect.h2: What you will get, and what you will not
expect.body: Better said up front than discovered later. The analysis returns **major and minor** chords. It does not return extensions: a seventh, a ninth or a sus4 present in the recording will come back as a plain chord. The result is a draft to correct, saving you the work of picking it out by ear — not a transcription.

how.body: The recording goes through three stages. The tracks are first separated, to isolate what carries the harmony and set aside drums and vocals. The harmony is then estimated bar by bar, along with tempo and key. Finally a split into sections is proposed, and identical bars grouped.

input.body: An audio file, or a link to an online video. The file is the more reliable route: fetching from a link depends on a third-party service that may refuse the request.

fix.body: Take it in this order. Check the key first: if that is wrong, everything else will be. Then check the split into sections, easier to recognise by ear than the chords. Finish with the doubtful bars, the ones where the chord changes midway — that is where the estimate goes wrong most often.

quota.body: Two analyses per month on the free plan. That counter is shared with photo transcription: two analyses in total, whichever route you take. Unlimited on Pro.

when.body: If the song already exists as a chart on a chord site, importing the text will give a better result in less time. If you have the score in front of you, a photo will be more faithful. Audio analysis is for the cases where all you have is the recording.

instrumentPage.lead: All {count} {instrumentLower} chords on Alviena, grouped by family. Every chord has its own page: the diagram, the notes it is built from, the shape in detail, and the charts on the site that use it.
instrumentPage.otherInstruments: The same chords on another instrument
instrumentPage.startLead: These are the chords that come up most often in the charts published on the site. Learning them {instrumentAt} before the rest opens up the largest part of the repertoire: the figure says how many charts each one appears in.
instrumentPage.startCount: These {count} chords are enough to play a good share of the catalogue. The rest of this page groups them by family, from the most common to the rarest.
instrumentPage.reading: Read the diagram as if the instrument were standing upright in front of you: the strings run vertically, the lowest on the left, and the horizontal bars are the frets. A dot marks a finger; a circle above a string means it rings open; a cross means it is not played. A thick bar across the top means the shape starts at the nut; otherwise the number on the left gives the fret of the first row shown. A solid bar across several strings is a barre: one finger lays them all down.
instrumentPage.linkFinder: Find a chord from its notes
instrumentPage.linkTranspose: Transpose a chart into another key

about.guitar: Six strings, tuned E A D G B E from low to high. Open shapes — the ones that let strings ring in the first few frets — are both the easiest and the loudest, which is why they come first. Barre chords follow: harder on the hand, but they slide along the neck, one shape giving twelve chords.
about.ukulele: Four strings tuned G C E A, with the quirk that the top string is not the lowest: that re-entrant tuning is what gives the ukulele its sound. Most chords take one to three fingers, which makes it the quickest string instrument to get under the hands.
about.mandolin: Four courses of two strings tuned in unison, G D A E like a violin. The fifth between courses makes shapes tighter than on a guitar and keeps chords close to their theoretical form: three or four notes, rarely more.
about.banjo: Five strings in open G, g D G B D, the fifth being a drone attached at the fifth fret: it is not fretted in a chord shape. The diagrams in this library therefore show the four strings the fretting hand actually uses.
about.piano: No neck, no fingering to work out: a piano chord is a stack of notes, and the keyboard shows it. Each page gives the exact notes to press, in the most common inversion. The same shape transposes by sliding the whole thing up or down as many semitones as needed.

chordPage.lead: The {chord} chord diagram {instrumentAt}, the notes it is built from, and the Alviena charts that use it.
chordPage.leadFrench: The {chord} chord diagram {instrumentAt} ({frenchChord}), the notes it is built from, the shape in detail, and the Alviena charts that use it.
chordPage.notesExplainer: {count, plural, one {The chord is built from a single pitch.} other {The chord is built from # distinct pitches.}} A shape may double them an octave apart: the same note then appears more than once without changing the chord.
chordPage.traitOpen: {count, plural, one {# open string} other {# open strings}}
chordPage.traitMuted: {count, plural, one {# muted string} other {# muted strings}}
chordPage.sheetsHeading: Songs to play with the {chord} chord {instrumentAt}
chordPage.sameFamilyHeading: The same colour, on another root

editorGuide.lead: A chart is built section by section, bar after bar. Here is how the editor works, and the shortcuts that save time.

sections.body: A chart is split into named sections: intro, verse, chorus, bridge, pre-chorus, solo, outro. Each carries its own repeat count, shown as “×2” next to its title, which saves copying the same progression eight times. Sections can be reordered by dragging, and duplicated in one click when a chorus returns with a variation.

measures.body: Each section has its own time signature. A 4/4 bar gives four beats, a 3/4 bar gives three. The signature is set per section, so a song whose bridge turns into a waltz needs no starting over.

durations.h2: A chord can last more or less than a beat
durations.body: Every cell takes an adjustable duration, from a quarter of a beat to four full beats, in quarter steps. Three buttons are enough: the left arrow absorbs the previous cell, the right arrow absorbs the next, and the divide symbol splits the cell in two. That is how you write two chords on one beat, or one chord held across a whole bar.

keyboard.body: Tab moves from one cell to the next, then down to the following bar. At the end of the last bar it creates a new one and steps into it: a whole chart can be typed without ever leaving the keyboard or clicking “add a bar”.

notation.body: You can type “Am” or “Lam”, “Fa#m7” or “F#m7”: French entry is recognised and converted. Display then follows each reader's preference, set in their profile — two musicians can read the same chart in two different notations.

mic.body: Rather than typing, you can play. The mic button listens, recognises the chord, writes it into the target cell and moves to the next. Silence acts as confirmation: play the chord, mute the strings, it is written. That is what makes it possible to write the same chord twice in a row, which a held chord could not distinguish.

finder.h2: Finding a chord whose name you don't know
finder.body: When you know the shape but not the name, the chord finder does the opposite of a dictionary: click the frets on the neck or the piano keys, and matching chords appear, ranked by closeness. One click inserts them into the cell.

custom.body: A chord whose suggested shape does not suit can be redrawn for the chart: open strings, muted strings, barre, starting fret. The custom shape travels with the chart, including in print and for anyone reading it.

metadata.body: Entering the title and artist looks up the tempo automatically and brings in the album artwork. The key is derived from the chart's own chords as soon as there are two: it therefore describes what is written, capo included, not the original recording. Both stay editable by hand, and a value you enter is never overwritten.

printGuide.lead: A chart is also read on paper, on a music stand, with no battery to run flat. The print layout is built for that.

layout.h2: A layout made for the page
layout.body: In print the interface disappears: no navigation bar, no buttons, no menus. What remains is the title, the artist, the key, the tempo and the chart. The layout targets A4 and avoids splitting a section in the middle when it could fit whole on the next page.

diagrams.body: Diagrams for the chords used can be printed at the top of the chart, or left out. The setting lives in your profile: turn it on for a song you are learning, off for a repertoire you know and want to keep to one page.

repeats.body: A second setting replaces identical sections with a short reminder instead of reprinting them. A song with three identical choruses then often fits on a single sheet instead of two. Again it is a choice: some prefer everything laid out on the stand.

colors.body: If you read in dark theme, printing switches to light on its own: black text on white. Nobody wants to empty a cartridge over a charcoal background, and a dark chart on paper is unreadable on a poorly lit stand.

pdf.body: There is no separate export button: the browser's print command offers “Save as PDF” as a destination. The resulting file matches what the printer would produce, and can be emailed or loaded onto a tablet.

sets.h2: A whole set in one file
sets.body: For a gig, printing songs one by one is tedious. A whole set exports as a single PDF, in setlist order, ready to bind or load onto a tablet. This bulk export is reserved for Pro accounts; printing a single chart stays open to everyone.

items: Pick your instrument: guitar, ukulele, mandolin, banjo, bass or piano.
Click the frets, or the keys, to place your fingers.
Matching chords appear as you go, closest first.
Click a result to hear it, and check by ear what the screen claims.

naming.h2: Why one shape has several names
naming.body: One set of notes often goes by several names, depending on which one you treat as the root. C E G A is C6 if you start from C, and Am7 if you start from A: same four sounds, both names correct.
naming.body2: The song decides, not the shape. The ranking puts the most common reading first, but the others stay on screen: they are not mistakes.

limits.body: It only searches the library shapes for the chosen instrument. An unusual position, musically sound, may return nothing: that does not mean it has no name.
limits.body2: It ignores inversions: a shape does not say which note is in the bass, while a slash chord like D/F# depends entirely on it.
